title: Peace and Security
summary: ## Meaning of peace

A king's painting contest: the winning picture showed a bird calmly feeding its young in a nest behind a roaring waterfall in a storm — peace does not mean the absence of noise or trouble, but staying calm in the midst of it. Peace is a social and political condition that ensures the development of individuals, society and the nation; a state of harmony with healthy relationships, social and economic welfare and equality, and a political order serving the interests of all. Between and within nations it is not merely the absence of war but also the presence of socio-cultural and economic understanding and unity.
## Meaning of security

Security is used at individual, institutional, regional, national and international levels. It means a secure condition, free from fear, and the safety of an individual, institution, region, nation or the world. In its most basic sense it means freedom from extremely dangerous threats, including threats to core values like human rights.

Peace and security are inseparable: together they are a condition in which individuals, institutions, regions, nations and the world move ahead without threat. Such nations are usually stable, democratic and respect human rights; conflict causes fear and hampers economic, social and political progress.
## Traditional and new notions

Traditional notion: threats of military attack by another nation to sovereignty, independence and territory. Remedies: bilateral agreements and treaties, stronger defence, troops on borders, balance of power through alliances, and international bodies like the UN.

New (non-traditional) notion: much broader — covers individuals, communities and humankind, not just nations; sees peace and security as a precondition of socio-economic development and human dignity; includes freedom from hunger, want, disease and epidemics, environmental degradation, exploitation and sub-human treatment. Threats include terrorism, insurgency, genocide, denial of human rights, epidemics, narcotics trade and irrational use of natural resources.
## Peace, democracy and development

They are mutually linked. Without peace, elections cannot be held, democratic institutions cannot work, citizens cannot participate, and no development is possible amid violence or war. In turn, democracies rarely go to war and remove causes of dissatisfaction through participation; development improves quality of life and removes the sense of deprivation that causes violence. The UN Millennium Development Goals (2000) saw peace and security as key to development; the 2005 World Summit said development, peace and security and human rights are interlinked and mutually reinforcing.
## India's approach

India faces external threats (wars with China and Pakistan) and internal ones (insurgency, Naxalism). The approach began in the freedom movement: leaders knew democracy and development need peace, pledged to promote international peace, supported anti-colonial and anti-racist movements, and chose a socialistic approach with social justice and secularism to prevent internal threats. Nehru (Columbia University, 1949): India's policy is not negative and neutral but positive, flowing from the freedom struggle and Gandhi's teachings.

The Constitution puts peace and security in the Directive Principles of State Policy — Article 51: the State shall promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, foster respect for international law and treaties, and encourage settlement of disputes by arbitration. This means the State should aim at peace and security while making laws and policies. Federalism and local governments prevent centralisation, which can cause regional discontent. Nationally India ensures liberty, equality, social justice, secularism and equal participation so that no section feels discriminated.
## Internal threats
Protests, strikes and bandhs are normal law-and-order matters in a democracy; terrorism, insurgency and the Naxalite movement are serious threats.

Terrorism: a criminal act to inflict dramatic and deadly injury on civilians and create an atmosphere of fear, generally for a political or ideological purpose — never justifiable (UN Security Council Resolution 1566, 2004). Examples: the Mumbai attack of 26 November 2008 (26/11); bomb blasts, firing in crowded places, hijacking planes to force release of jailed terrorists.

Insurgency: an armed rebellion against the constituted government — some with political motives (secessionist groups in J&K and Assam), some for social and economic justice (groups in Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura); many get support from neighbouring countries.

Naxalite movement: began in March 1967 at Naxalbari (West Bengal) under Charu Mazumdar and Kanu Sanyal as a peasant uprising; later spread to about 125 districts in 12 States. Naxals attack police and officials, oppose development (roads) in forests and hold 'kangaroo courts'. Root cause: social discrimination and economic deprivation of tribals, SCs and dalits who have not received the fruits of development.

Government strategy: support global efforts against terrorism and seek help after attacks; diplomatic pressure on Pakistan and neighbours to stop support to terrorists; treaties with Myanmar and Bangladesh against insurgent support; Naxalism treated not just as law and order but as a socio-economic problem — faster development and bringing youth into the mainstream.
## India and international peace

Objectives of India's foreign policy: (1) freedom in policy formulation; (2) promotion of international peace and security; (3) good relations with all, especially neighbours; (4) support to the UN; (5) disarmament and opposition to colonialism, imperialism and racism; (6) cooperation among developing nations.

Non-alignment: during the Cold War between the US-led western bloc and the Soviet-led communist bloc (a bipolar world), India refused to join either military alliance and judged each issue on its merits. It was not neutrality, non-involvement or isolationism. Founders of NAM: Nehru, Tito (Yugoslavia) and Nasser (Egypt) (with Nkrumah, Sukarno). Relevance after the Cold War: a check on a unipolar world, a forum for North–South dialogue and South–South cooperation, and a voice for UN reform.

Support to the UN: India is one of the 51 founding members; it supports UN efforts for peace, peacekeeping and disarmament, wants disputes settled by negotiation, and seeks an active UN role in development. India has a strong case for permanent membership of the Security Council — its size, democracy, growing economy, peacekeeping record and leadership of developing countries.

vsa: Peace cannot exist where people live under threat, and security is meaningless without harmony. Together they create a condition where individuals, institutions, nations and the world move ahead without threat; conflict creates fear and hampers progress.
How does the new notion of security differ from the traditional notion? Give two points.

(1) The traditional notion is about military threats to a nation's territory and sovereignty; the new one covers threats like terrorism, hunger, disease, environmental damage and denial of human rights. (2) The new notion focuses on individuals and humankind, not just States, and treats security as a precondition of development and dignity.
What contribution did the freedom movement make to India's approach to peace and security?

Leaders realised democracy and development need peace, pledged that free India would promote international peace, supported anti-colonial and anti-racist movements, and chose social justice and secularism to prevent internal threats.
Why did India adopt the policy of non-alignment?

To keep its independence in foreign policy during the Cold War by not joining the US or Soviet military blocs, to judge each issue on merit, to promote world peace and to focus on its own development with help from all.
sa: Why are peace and security essential for the progress of individuals, nations and the world? Explain.

(1) Development needs peace — no economic or social progress is possible amid violence or war; resources go to defence instead. (2) Democracy needs peace — elections, democratic institutions and people's participation can work only in peaceful conditions. (3) Individuals can live with dignity, free from fear, enjoy rights and plan their lives; at world level, peace allows trade and cooperation.
Describe the strategy of the Government of India to deal with terrorism, insurgency and the Naxalite movement.

(1) Terrorism — support and seek international cooperation and put diplomatic pressure on Pakistan and neighbours to stop support to terrorist groups. (2) Insurgency — tackle it diplomatically through treaties with Myanmar and Bangladesh to stop help to insurgents, along with security measures. (3) Naxalism — treated as a socio-economic problem, not just law and order: speed up development in affected areas and bring youth into the mainstream.
Explain the relationship between peace and security on one hand and democracy and development on the other.

(1) Without peace elections and democratic institutions cannot function and development cannot take place. (2) Democracies rarely go to war and give all citizens a chance to participate, removing causes of discontent. (3) Development improves quality of life and removes the sense of deprivation that leads to protests and violence; the 2005 World Summit called them interlinked and mutually reinforcing.
What are the causes of the Naxalite movement? How can it be solved?

Causes: social discrimination and economic deprivation of tribals, SCs and dalits; the fruits of development not reaching them; disputes over land and forests. Solutions: faster development — roads, schools, jobs — in affected areas; land reforms and protection of forest rights; dialogue to bring youth into the mainstream along with firm action against violence.
Explain any three basic objectives of India's foreign policy.

(1) Promotion of international peace and security and support to the United Nations. (2) Good relations with all nations, especially neighbours, while keeping freedom in policy formulation (non-alignment). (3) Disarmament; opposition to colonialism, imperialism and racism; and cooperation among developing nations.
How has India supported the United Nations? Why does India deserve permanent membership of the Security Council?

Support: a founding member; contributes troops to UN peacekeeping; supports disarmament and settlement of disputes by negotiation; wants an active UN role in development of poor countries. Claim: largest democracy and huge population, fast-growing economy, long peacekeeping record and leadership of developing countries.
la: What is meant by peace and security? How is the traditional notion different from the new notion? Explain.

Peace is a condition of harmony ensuring development of individuals, society and the nation — not merely absence of war but presence of socio-cultural and economic understanding. Security is freedom from fear and dangerous threats, including threats to human rights. Traditional notion: (1) focuses on military threats from another nation; (2) concerns the nation's sovereignty and territory; (3) remedies are treaties, defence build-up, alliances and balance of power. New notion: (4) broader — terrorism, insurgency, genocide, epidemics, narcotics, environmental damage; (5) centred on individuals and humankind; (6) a precondition for development and human dignity — freedom from hunger, want, disease and exploitation.
Examine the relevance of the Non-Aligned Movement and India's role in maintaining world peace through the UN.

NAM: (1) founded by Nehru, Tito and Nasser during the Cold War so new nations could stay free of military blocs; (2) after the Cold War it checks the dominance of a unipolar world; (3) it is a forum for North–South dialogue and South–South cooperation, raising the bargaining power of developing countries; (4) it presses for UN reform. UN: (5) India, a founding member, supports UN peacekeeping and disarmament and wants disputes solved by talks; (6) it seeks a UN role in development and a permanent seat in a reformed Security Council.
